title: Parents say this N.S. driving school ‘ghosted’ them after they paid hundreds of dollars
summary: Several parents with children enrolled in Marshall Law Driving Academy say they feel blindsided by its sudden closure last week after each paying the company hundreds of dollars.

image.caption: Allison Wheaton is one of five parents CBC News spoke to about their similar experiences dealing with Marshall Law Driving Academy before its sudden closure on Nov. 10, 2026. (Dave Laughlin/CBC)

blocks.text: Nova Scotia
Several parents with children enrolled in Marshall Law Driving Academy say they feel blindsided by its sudden closure last week after each paying the company hundreds of dollars.
Marshall Law Driving Academy closed suddenly on Nov. 10 with students in the middle of training
Allison Wheaton says her family skipped a summer vacation this year so she could afford to put one of her children in driving school.
The single mother of two, who lives in Newport, N.S., says she paid $840 for her oldest daughter to complete online training and 10 hours of driving lessons from the Marshall Law Driving Academy.
But when Wheaton tried to schedule the first lesson, she says she could no longer get a hold of the company’s owner and main instructor, Neal Marshall.

“He didn't answer the phone. It was actually disconnected. And then I emailed him. There was no response and my text messages never ever did make it through. So, it came to a quick halt,” said Wheaton.
“I feel quite helpless. I didn't expect to be ghosted.”
Several parents with children who were enrolled in Marshall Law Driving Academy say they feel blindsided by its sudden closure last week after each paying the company hundreds of dollars.

A Facebook group called 'People Affected by Marshall Law Driving Academy' was created on Nov. 11 and has approximately 300 members sharing similar experiences they've had with owner Neal Marshall. (CBC)
They say while their children were in the school it was difficult getting in touch with Marshall, scheduling driving lessons and getting receipts after handing over the money.
When students were able to schedule lessons, the parents say sometimes Marshall just wouldn’t show up.
Jenni Dayringer, who lives in Amherst, says the instructor always had an excuse when he didn’t pick up her daughter.
“I was like, ‘Did we, like, make a mistake on the timing?' And he said, ‘No, my car broke down,’” Dayringer said.
“The next one that was to happen, he said he was in the hospital. He pulled stitches,” she said.
School has been doing this for years, parent says
Marshall has not responded to multiple attempts by CBC News to contact him.
A group on Facebook titled "People Affected by Marshall Law Driving Academy” has nearly 300 members.
CBC News spoke to five of them who shared similar experiences dealing with Marshall.
“It’s the same story you’ve probably heard numerous times … last minute cancellations, not available to do the lessons,” said Marc Priddle, who lives in Enfield.
Priddle’s son started lessons with Marshall in 2021, he says, and the problems started almost immediately.
A spokesperson for the province says Neal Marshall applied for a licence for another driving school but it was not approved. (Dan Jardine/CBC)
He says he was astonished to hear other customers say they were having similar experiences with the driving school years after he dealt with them.
“They’ve been in this business of making it difficult for kids to get what they paid for at least five years,” he said.
Priddle said he received a refund after leaving several poor reviews about the driving school online.
"[Marshall] agreed to refund me if I would stop commenting on his personal advertising posts about my experience," he said.
Marshall has another driving school, but no licence
Marshall gave notice to the province on Nov. 10 that he was ceasing operations, which led to his licence being cancelled, according to a spokesperson with the Department of Public Works.
The spokesperson said no reason was given for why the business ceased operations. Marshall is listed as the operator of Fall River Driving School on the province’s registry of joint stocks website.
He did apply for a licence for that school, but it was not approved, according to the spokesperson.
“Under the new Traffic Safety Act, government can consider previous business conduct before approving an application for a new licence,” the provincial spokesperson said in an email.
The spokesperson said the province is currently working to help find alternatives for students who were unable to complete their driver training.
